prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: lumbar puncture below an expanded cord with near-complete effacement of the subarachnoid space risks neurological deterioration (spinal coning).
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established

Do not attribute the lesion to an NF1-associated low-grade glioma or to inflammatory myelitis and defer tissue: an expansile enhancing intramedullary mass with an exophytic component and rapid progression needs a histomolecular diagnosis.
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to spinal neurosurgery for open biopsy through a cervical laminectomy, with debulking only where it can be done safely, targeting the enhancing intramedullary segment; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis including H3 K27 status (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic cord oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when cord compression is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.
Monitor for respiratory and bulbar compromise given the high cervical and medullary extent (vital capacity, swallowing, neurological checks), escalating to high-dependency care if it develops.

Stop the combined oral contraceptive, since estrogen adds to the venous thromboembolism risk of a high-grade glioma and of spinal surgery; offer a copper intrauterine device or a progestogen-only method, and confirm a negative pregnancy test before surgery and any chemoradiotherapy.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at 34 with KPS 70 the standard is radiotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide, with the dose limited by spinal cord tolerance (about 50.4 to 54 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions rather than 60 Gy), and a clinical trial where available (EANO 2021).

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Lucia Navarro is a 34-year-old right-handed woman with a longstanding history of neurofibromatosis type 1 who presents to the emergency department with a four-day history of rapidly progressive motor weakness involving her right arm and sensory disturbances affecting both lower extremities. She reports that approximately four days ago, she noticed difficulty gripping her coffee cup with her right hand while preparing for work. Over the following 24 hours, the weakness progressed to involve the entire right upper extremity, making it difficult for her to use her computer mouse or hold objects securely. Concurrently, she developed an uncomfortable tingling and numbness sensation in both feet that ascended to involve her calves and thighs over the next two days. She describes a tight, band-like squeezing sensation around her mid-chest that worsens with deep breathing, which she initially attributed to anxiety. Two days ago, she noticed increasing stiffness and heaviness in both legs when climbing the stairs to her apartment, and her partner observed that her gait had become noticeably stiff and unsteady. She has also experienced a new electric shock-like sensation radiating down her spine and into her legs when she bends her neck forward, which she finds alarming. She denies any preceding fever, recent infections, vaccinations, or systemic symptoms. There has been no bowel or bladder dysfunction, although she notes some mild urinary urgency that she had attributed to her increased fluid intake. She has had no headache, visual changes, facial weakness, difficulty swallowing, nausea, vomiting or hiccups. She denies any recent trauma or unusual physical activity. Her migraines have been at their usual baseline frequency. She reports that her NF1-related symptoms, including her cutaneous neurofibromas, have been stable for years, and her childhood optic glioma has not required treatment. She is particularly worried because her father, who also has NF1, developed a large plexiform neurofibroma that required surgical intervention, and her paternal grandmother died of a brain tumor. She has not had a neurological assessment or spinal imaging in over three years.
